title: Taste at scale
description: The agency model was always a headcount problem. More clients meant more people. Margins stayed thin because the work couldn’t scale faster than the team. Every studio I watched operate ran into the same ceiling: the work was good, the growth was slow, and the business was fragile. I built Nirmata to see whether one person with the right tools and judgment could do what used to require a team of eight. The answer is yes. With a few things worth saying out loud. The economics changed Software used to be expensive to build . Three things collapsed at roughly the same time: the cost of execution, the cost of coordination, and the cost of custom software. When those three things were expensive, you needed specialists for each, and a project manager to stitch them together. When they got cheap, the specialists became overhead. AI writing code is the obvious story. The less obvious one is what that does to project economics. . A custom interface that used to require two weeks of a senior developer’s time can come together in days. A design system that would have needed a dedicated sprint now gets built alongside the thing it governs. The friction between design and development, the handoff cost that every agency has tried and failed to eliminate, shrinks to almost nothing when one person is handling both ends with AI in the loop. That’s the mechanical case for Nirmata. Design and development as a single continuous process, owned by one studio, delivered at a pace the traditional model structurally can’t match. Where product work actually breaks Most product work fails at the boundary between disciplines. The designer doesn’t understand what’s expensive to build. The developer doesn’t know which edge cases the design was trying to solve. The PM is translating between them and losing signal in both directions. By the time something ships, it’s a negotiated object, shaped more by coordination cost than by the original intent. Whoever can hold design, engineering, and product decisions in the same head and act on all three without waiting for a meeting will outshine a committee every time. What gets cheaper is execution. What stays expensive is knowing what to build, why it matters, and whether the thing you shipped is actually working. Coding agents accelerate shipping, which puts pressure on the part that teams have always struggled with most. That part has stayed stubbornly manual, even as everything around it gets automated. A ticket manager who creates tasks and tracks status is overhead in this model. Judgment isn’t. A studio that controls the full cycle removes most of the translation steps. The thinking that shapes the design is the same thinking that decides how it gets built. That continuity shows up in the work. What the freed space is for The design founder era is partly about aesthetics and partly about this. Founders who can hold the visual and the technical in the same head reliably build things that feel coherent. The interface and the system underneath it are solving the same problem, in the same register. When agents handle the implementation, something shifts. The cognitive overhead of writing code drops out, and the mental space it occupied goes somewhere else. For me, it goes toward the psychology of what gets built. Why does this pattern create anxiety? Why does this flow cause people to abandon? What does this decision cost the user versus what it earns the product? I’ve spent years building a library of over a hundred psychological principles that apply directly to product decisions, documented at 1984.design . Loss aversion, cognitive load, the peak-end rule, decision fatigue. Applied directly, they separate a feature that serves users from one that extracts from them. Dark patterns (aka deceptive patterns ) exist because most builders never slow down enough to ask whether what they’re shipping is actually good for the person on the other end. Coding with agents creates that space. The speed is a side effect. The more important thing is what you can think about while the code gets written. The caution YC’s Spring 2026 request list named it: AI-native agencies running at software-level margins, same output, none of the coordination cost. A model that treats headcount as a variable, not a fixed input. Nirmata was built on that assumption before the framing existed. AI-written code still needs someone accountable for what it does. Security, reliability, IP, those don’t disappear because the code came fast. I treat oversight as part of the work, not something you add at the end. What remains AI absorbed the execution layer. What’s left is editorial work: knowing what to build, recognizing when it’s right, deciding when to stop. The design bar will keep rising alongside this. Builders who ship more can iterate faster, which means the gap between good taste and no taste compounds over time. AI also improves its own design output , so even companies for whom design wasn’t a priority will get access to better defaults. The premium moves entirely to taste, the ability to recognize what works, what doesn’t, and why. A one-person studio doing the full cycle lives in that space. Which problems are worth solving. Which tradeoffs to accept. How to hold a coherent vision from the first conversation to the thing that ships. AI handles the rest. That’s why I’m building Nirmata . Thanks for reading. — B.

title: mostrando o meu quarto ☕️🐢
description: Essa é uma edição diferente. Ninguém perguntou… mas lembrei o quanto gosto de saber onde e como as pessoas criam. Nosso repertório, referências e estímulos nutrem o processo criativo com ideias… …e a falta, diferença ou improviso das ferramentas mudam nossas escolhas e estética - e pode ser isso que nos diferencia :¬) Por isso, a edição de hoje mostra o meu novo espaço inacabado: me mudei há duas semanas! 👁️ Aviso: não arrumei NADA antes de tirar as fotos, hihi! Você vai ver o mundo real pós mudança, sem a “maquiagem” que costuma ser usada antes de mostrar coisas online. O Ministério da Criatividade adverte: os links abaixo são links de afiliados (sempre que escrevo afiliados, penso em afilhados). Caso queira comprar algo, avalie se realmente faz sentido dentro do seu contexto e orçamento; nenhuma ferramenta te torna, automaticamente, uma pessoa mais criativa. Caso decida comprar, recomendo buscar preços melhores, porque linkei as primeiras opções que encontrei :) Começando pelos objetos que mais encosto sem luva: esse mouse e esse teclado. Tô brincando sobre a luva. Nunca uso. A não ser que eu jogue de goleiro - e eu nunca jogo de goleiro. Ao lado deles, um Macbook Pro e esse microfone (ambos de 2020) e um 2º monitor ultrawide da LG. Escrevo numa mesa que levanta porque gosto de trabalhar umas horas de pé :¬) Como vai ficar a parede? Tô entre reconstruir essa parede ou testar algo novo. Agora, saindo de casa…. Hoje, 70% dos meus dias não começam trabalhando aqui. Criei o ritual de ir num café depois de deixar minha filha na creche. É uma forma de focar na escrita (e, depois, em tarefas chatinhas) num lugar onde me sinto bem. Me considero (muito!) sortudo por, hoje, ter essa flexibilidade de trabalhar remotamente. Foi um sonho que conduziu minhas escolhas profissionais e me fez mudar de carreira 2x. Se você me lê, você faz parte disso. Muito obrigado 💛 Agora, voltando pra casa: ”desculpa a bagunça”, hihi! Como combino o analógico e digital, quase tudo nasce da impressora Ecotank da Epson que ainda não me deixou na mão :¬) Minhas poesias visuais são criadas no Illustrator e vídeos editados no Premiere Pro (ou pelo Zé ). Fotografo tudo com meu celular, antes de editar usando Photoshop. Uso papéis brancos levemente mais grossos que o normal porque são melhores de rasgar - e brinco com os coloridos de vez em quando. Ah, a caneta que mais uso é a boa e velha BIC: sempre a preta, porque a azul me lembra a época da escola (zero saudade). Ela é mais pra escrever e/ou brainstormar com as mãos :¬) Mas, nas criações, costumo gravitar muito pro lápis 6B (sem apontar, porque curto a textura rústica) e canetinhas de pontas finas da STAEDTLER. Pra fotografar, combino luz natural com uma softbox, que quero trocar por algo menos volumoso. Por que? “Como criar com menos “trecos” ao meu redor?” é uma pergunta que tem me motiva, hehe. Mas sem exageros! :¬) Busco um equilíbrio entre ter menos coisas e, ao mesmo tempo, conveniência na hora de criar. Com o tempo, o quartinho vai ganhando forma e essa bagunça aí atrás vai abrir espaço pra um sofá e etc. Tô sem pressa pra arrumar e decorar tudo: minha família e o trabalho são prioridades. Caso você tenha curiosidade de ver meu espaço antigo, você pode assistir meu vlog . O vlog é desatualizado? Muito :¬) O Ministério da Criatividade adverte (de novo!): eu não era pai, ainda não tinha voltado a comer carne (depois de 9 anos), ia menos pra cafés… a rotina mudou bastante! Se você também publicar suas ideias pela internet: curioso pra saber onde e como você cria :¬) garimpos 💾 um calendário retrô feito num Mac antigo. 🧱 tô fascinado pelos mosaicos dessa artista . 👟 só pra quem tem pouco tempo pra ir na academia. 🍏 pra assistir e pensar quais são as variáveis de toque humano na sua forma de se expressar. pum Esse é um pum pra você jogar no seu grupo favorito de WhatsApp: Se você pudesse escolher apenas uma foto por mês para contar a história do seu ano até agora … quais seriam essas fotos? Uma linha do tempo visual e com histórias, hehe :¬) As fotos podem acompanhar áudios e mensagens… ou serem uma desculpa pra marcar um papo sobre elas num café. C om carinho, Tiago 🐢 P.S. alerta de vlog desatualizado aqui embaixo, hehe :¬)

title: What A Coincidence
description: * This was meant to go out yesterday, but there was a glitch on my end. Sorry! * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for September is STRIPES. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . So many great contributions! Check it out ! “ coincidence ,” by K Bahr on Flickr “A coincidence, after all, has to be noticed.“ Dear friend of TAoN Suzanne M sent me a link the other day to a deep-dive article about coincidences . I’d never given this subject much thought, but it turned out to be pretty interesting. And as Suzanne detected, there was a noticing/attention angle that I couldn’t help dwelling on. A coincidence, after all, has to be noticed. If I walk past a childhood friend I haven’t seen in 20 years in some airport where neither of us lives, one of us has to notice the other for the coincidence to “count,” as it were. In some ways, “ the amazing thing is not that these things occur, it’s that we notice them, ” according to David Spiegelhalter, a professor at the University of Cambridge who studies such things, as quoted in Julie Beck’s’ Atlantic article. You could say that being more attentive leads to registering more coincidences. Spiegelhalter, the article notes, has a website where people can submit their coincidence experiences, and claims to have collected something like 5,000 of them. The most common form is “ finding a link with someone you meet .” Obviously, this suggests that people who are looking for connections — who are open, curious, attentive to others — are more likely to find unexpected ones. “Coincidences never happen to me at all, because I never notice anything,” Spiegelhalter says (somewhat jokingly). “I never talk to anybody on trains. If I’m with a stranger, I don’t try to find a connection with them … .” I admit it never really occurred to me that there could be coincidence-friendly types . But Beck also cites another researcher who has found that certain personality traits are linked to experiencing more coincidences—people who describe themselves as religious or spiritual, people who are self-referential (or likely to relate information from the external world back to themselves), and people who are high in meaning-seeking are all coincidence-prone. The article goes on to explore everything from Jung’s idea of synchronicity to popular notions of the paranormal. Possibly the opposite of missing coincidences is reading too much meaning into mere chance occurrences that look like something more. The world shapes our attention, but sometimes attention shapes our world — for better or worse! That said, I’m attracted to this idea that “finding a link with someone you meet” is the most-reported form of coincidence. It’s a nice frame for chatting with someone new: Be curious, be open — and look for a happy coincidence or two. Leave a comment Thank you Suzanne! Noticing is about other people, too. title: Wild, As In Harmonious
description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for September is STRIPES. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . So many great contributions! Check it out ! “You need to go out into the world and look.” If you pay attention to the idea of paying attention, you have no doubt encountered the words of Mary Oliver, from her poems, essays, interviews. Oliver attracted fans ranging from John Waters to Oprah, from Stephen Colbert to Lucy Dacus. In The Art of Noticing book, I quoted from her poem “ Sometimes ”: Instructions for living a life: Pay attention. Be astonished. Tell about it. But the truth is, I didn’t really know much about Oliver’s life, and even my familiarity with her work was pretty thin. So I was very excited to see the new documentary about her, Mary Oliver: Saved By the Beauty of the World, via the PBS series American Masters. You can watch on the PBS site , or on YouTube . I recommend it! The documentary covers Oliver’s career as well her personal life, traumas included. (The title borrows from her line: “I got saved by poetry, and I got saved by the beauty of the world.”) I won’t attempt to summarize the whole thing, but I’ll share some of of the TAoN- relevant highlights. Oliver grew up in Ohio, an outsider drawn mostly to the natural world and “dead poets.” She preferred noticing to being noticed. Later, in her 20s, she learned from the intensity with which her partner, photographer Molly Malone Cook, interacted with others. Another of her familiar quotations: “ Attention without feeling … is only a report. ” Oliver and Cook lived in Provincetown, where Oliver continued her practice, attentive and poetic, walking the same paths to discover what she missed before. In time, she won major awards, and a significant audience, but to some extent the literary establishment pigeonholed her as someone who basically just went for walks and wrote about it. One person in the documentary calls her an icon of the hermit life. But that’s not the whole story. “You need to go out into the world and look,” the poet Mark Doty says in the documentary, and that’s exactly what Oliver was doing — even if it was in the nearby woods. Her appreciation of the natural world was no retreat. It was the opposite. “ Attention is the beginning of devotion, ” as she (famously) wrote in the title essay of her collection Upstream . This is perhaps her central lesson for those of us who care to go out into the world land look. “You can get ecstatic over a box of matches,” she remarks in one interview clip. And in other she makes the point I love the most: “If you love something, you give it a lot of attention. And if you give something a lot of attention, you very often learn to love it.” Yet another widely quoted Oliver line is her poetic question : “ what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life? ” Her own life might not sound “wild” in the way we commonly use that word. But if you don’t have time for the whole documentary, check out the clip below discussing her poem “ Wild Geese ” — and ultimately pointing out that wild can also mean natural, harmonious. title: #303 Guia do LinkedIn sobre aparecer na IA
description: Se você cuida das redes de uma marca, vale se preparar: a propaganda eleitoral começa neste domingo, dia 16, e o clima tende a ficar mais sensível nos comentários, nas menções e até em conteúdos que não têm nenhuma relação direta com política. Na prática, é hora de combinar com o time: o que responder, quando não entrar na conversa, quais temas exigem atenção e quem acionar se surgir uma crise. As próprias plataformas têm até domingo para apresentar ao TSE seus planos de transparência, moderação e prevenção de riscos. Entenda o que muda. TL;DR Resumo do resumo das principais notícias da semana 🧠 A descoberta está mudando: Reddit influencia compras, anúncios chegam ao ChatGPT e aparecer na resposta vira uma preocupação. 🧠 No LinkedIn, conhecimento vale mais do que número de seguidores para conquistar visibilidade nas buscas por IA. 🧠 Meta testa opção paga “ Aumentar seguidores automaticamente ” no Meta One. 🧠 E o novo visual do instagram , hein? MANDA NEWS Novidades da semana. A Similarweb explica como crescer mesmo com as buscas sem clique e reforça uma mudança importante para o conteúdo: acompanhar se a marca aparece na resposta. Governo determina s uspensão de lives do Discord após morte de menina ao vivo. A IA pode adicionar quase R$ 1 trilhão à economia brasileira até 2030, segundo estudo encomendado pela OpenAI. A maior parte desse impacto virá do aumento da produtividade dos trabalhadores . Record: Esse vídeo do MrBeast é o TikTok mais repostado de todos os tempos . MANDA DADOS Estudo destaca a influência do Reddit nas decisões de compra Um estudo da Rival Technologies aponta que 72% da Gen Z já deixaram de comprar, seguir ou apoiar uma marca por causa do uso de IA no marketing. Para pensar: A s proibições de adolescentes nas redes sociais na Austrália estão tendo pouco efeit o, já que os adolescentes continuam a se apresentar burlando das restrições. A Adobe ouviu 850 pequenos negócios e profissionais autônomos nos EUA e descobriu que quase metade edita bastante o conteúdo feito com ajuda de IA antes de publicar. O estudo reforça que personalidade é o que impede as marcas de parecerem todas iguais Primeiro estudo empírico dos anúncios dentro do ChatGPT. 🧠 Anúncios entram em outro momento da jornada: No ChatGPT, ele surge enquanto a pessoa está tentando entender uma situação, tomar uma decisão ou resolver um problema. NOVIDADES DAS REDES INSTAGRAM Depois de dez anos, a plataforma atualizou o logotipo escrito, criou novas fontes e reorganizou seu sistema visual, mas manteve intacto o ícone colorido que todo mundo reconhece. O Instagram mostrou o processo de criação neste carrossel . FACEBOOK/META No novo Creator Studio , a pessoa pode perguntar à IA quando publicar, o que a audiência está dizendo e quais comentários merecem resposta. Assinantes do Meta One estão recebendo recursos como botão de seguir maior nos Reels, convites automáticos para quem interage com os posts (chamaram esse recurso de “ganhar seguidores automaticamente” ), perfis aprimorados e mais ferramentas de IA no Messenger. Meta testa otimizar campanhas para leads que realmente avançam. Uma das novidades permite definir uma sequência. Por exemplo, preencher o formulário e depois agendar uma reunião, e só atribui resultado quando as duas ações acontecem na ordem indicada. Agora, a nunciantes podem criar públicos personalizado s usados exclusivamente para exclusão. E que não podem ser reaproveitados depois na segmentação. Meta publica guias de marketing de férias Depois de casos de homens usando os Ray-Ban Meta para filmar mulheres sem consentimento, o produto ganhou o apelido de “óculos de tarado”. Agora, um movimento brasileiro pressiona Bruna Marquezine, embaixadora da Ray-Ban, a se posicionar WHATSAPP Meta apresenta alertas atualizados de golpes chegando ao WhatsApp LINKED IN Conteúdo muito bom: Segundo o novo guia do LinkedIn sobre visibilidade na busca por IA , 75% das citações do LinkedIn encontradas pela Meltwater vieram de perfis pessoais, e o número de seguidores teve menos importância do que a demonstração de conhecimento. YOUTUBE YouTube dificulta a monetização. A plataforma dobrou a exigência de horas assistidas para creators começarem a ganhar dinheiro. Menos botões , mais espaço para o conteúdo no YouTube REDDIT O Reddit compartilha insights para profissionais de marketing de viagens KWAI O Kwai abriu uma central de informações para as eleições A página é desenvolvida em parceria com o TSE . GOOGLE Google Ads e Analytics adicionam mais ferramenta s de IA Por hoje é isso. Beijo no 🧠 e até semana que vem!

title: viagem no tempo (em dupla) ☕️🐢
description: Bora viajar no tempo? :¬) Começando por 2011. Estava na faculdade e decidi enviar emails pra 80+ estúdios de design. “Eeeita, Tiago! :o O que você queria?” Uma hora de conversa sobre um tema que mexia (muito!) comigo: COMO essas pessoas ganhavam dinheiro… criando?! Principalmente, no início do projeto?! :o Foram 20+ conversas :’) Aprendi MUITO e, sem saber, dei o 1º passo de uma caminhada longa. Corta pra 2026: Ontem, enquanto encaixotava livros (vou me mudar!), esbarrei com um que MARATONEI em 2012 . E, nessa época, nem tinha o hábito de ler, viu? Adivinha o tema dele? :¬) O livro mergulhava nos bastidores de quem vive da criação e como cada pessoa navega isso. Acho bonito ver como, até hoje, esse tema me fascina e energiza. Ouço podcasts, vídeos no Youtube, etc. Épocas diferentes, mesma curiosidade. Por que isso importa? :¬) Lembrar desses momentos despretensiosos onde a gente explorava o que atiçava nossa curiosidade tem um efeito lindo: Porque visualizando como esses exemplos impactaram o presente , a gente começa a se convencer de que vale a pena se permitir explorá-los. Hoje, fazer algo sem função, improdutivo, ou que não ajuda na carreira é visto como perda de tempo por muita gente. Pra quem ainda pensa assim, essas ”evidências” do passado podem ajudar a dar mais uma chance pra experimentos, pro lúdico, pro brincar :¬) Por isso, deixo uma pergunta que, apesar de não ter proteína ou fibras, vem com zero calorias: Olhando pra trás: você largou algo que atiçava a sua curiosidade e ainda poderia estar na sua rotina? E caso não tenha largado: como isso estava na sua rotina antes? E como é agora? :¬) garimpos 💛 escutar com presença é uma arte :) 👁️ uma ideia legal de como decorar sua casa. 🥑 máquina de escrever + desenhos = esse livro. 🪐 esse mapa do mundo fez eu perceber coisas novas. 🍜 esse vídeo me faz sentir nostalgia-do-que-nunca-vivi. pum Esse é um pum sobre hobbies . Você tem feito o que quer fazer no tempo livre? Ou escolheu o que é mais instragramável? 👀 Mostrar a nossa vida num ambiente digital é uma das formas de projetar a nossa personalidade pro mundo. Por isso, existe o risco de até os hobbies - que deveriam ser prazerosos - ganharem uma camada extra de julgamento. O que o meu hobby comunica sobre mim? Que pertenço ao grupo X? Que não sigo modinha? Que tenho disciplina? Que sou culto? Que sou fútil? Você tem protegido os seus hobbies de julgamentos? :¬) Com carinho, Tiago 🐢

It comes from a short story callled “ Kim’s Game, ” by Sadia Shepard, published in The New Yorker earlier this year. In the story, a character recalls a childhood game that his father evidently took from Rudyard Kipling’s Kim : “My father would arrange a handful of objects on a tray—an old coin, a ribbon, a rock, a thimble, that sort of thing—and ask me to memorize them. Then he’d cover the tray with a newspaper and ask me to describe what I remembered. Sometimes, he’d take something away to see if I noticed . In the Kipling novel, the game is part of Kim’s training to be a spy.” This turns out to have become a well-known game , played (with variations) by children, the Cub Scouts , the military, and others. It actually sounds like a fun exercise — and also potentially a great assignment, particularly for a writing class. (And for the record it does sound like decent spy training, too.) title: Default Bias: Who chose your settings?
description: When a choice arrives with one option already set, most people leave it in place, regardless of whether it reflects their actual preference. The friction of changing something, combined with the implicit signal that the pre-set option is normal or recommended, produces consistent gravity toward the status quo. The mechanism runs through several channels at once. Loss aversion makes changing a default feel like risking something already owned. Implied endorsement suggests the default is a reasonable choice, so selecting it requires less justification. And the cognitive cost of evaluating alternatives encourages people to accept the existing state. These forces compound, especially in low-stakes or unfamiliar decisions where people lack strong preferences to override them. Default bias appears across organ donation programs, retirement savings enrollment, privacy settings, and software configuration. In each case, the same population of people produces dramatically different outcomes depending on which option requires action and which requires inaction. The default does not just simplify the interface. It determines the outcome for a large share of users. In design A user opens a new account and immediately lands in a signup flow. Before they have formed any preferences, the product has already decided: marketing emails are on, data sharing is enabled, notifications fire at full volume. The user clicks through, and the defaults stay. Default bias means the designer’s pre-set choices become most users’ permanent choices, whether or not those choices were made with the user’s benefit in mind. This places significant weight on the moment a default is chosen. Every pre-selected option is effectively a policy decision applied to the full user base. Designers who understand this use defaults to serve the majority, while keeping alternatives reachable. Those who ignore it discover that their defaults reflect internal convenience or business incentives rather than user needs. Applications in digital products Set the default communication preference to the least intrusive option, then let users escalate: email digests before individual notifications, not the reverse. When offering a free-to-paid upgrade, pre-select the plan that fits the user’s current usage, not the highest-tier plan, so the default reflects their situation. Place the destructive or irreversible action as the non-default: require an affirmative click to delete, unsubscribe, or share data, rather than treating those as pre-selected states. In onboarding forms, default empty fields to blank rather than placeholder values that users might submit without reading. On privacy and data settings, default to the most private configuration and present expansion as a deliberate user choice, not a correction of a setting they already “agreed to.” When a setting has a best-fit value for most users, pre-select it with a visible label like “Recommended” so the default carries transparent reasoning rather than hidden authority. Industry examples Countries with automatic organ donation enrollment see consent rates above 90%. Countries that require a positive registration act see rates below 20%. Same populations, different defaults. Thaler and Benartzi documented a similar pattern in 401(k) enrollment in 2003. Companies that switched retirement plans to automatic enrollment saw participation jump from around 50% to over 90%. Employees could still remove themselves. Most did not. Microsoft pre-selected telemetry and automatic update settings in Windows 10 that collected substantial user data. Changing them required navigating several menus. Few users did. Google enabled AI-assisted email completion in Gmail by default for all users. Adoption was high not because users chose it, but because disabling it required a deliberate action most skipped. Apple’s App Tracking Transparency, released in 2021, shifted ad tracking from an on-by-default state to an explicit prompt. Consent rates dropped from an estimated 70% to under 30%. No one changes what they don’t notice Changing a default requires two things most people avoid at the same time: forming a preference and acting on it. The pre-set option eliminates both requirements. People accept it without deliberating, often without noticing the choice was made. This is not a failure of attention, rather a rational response to cognitive load . When a decision is low-salience and the default seems reasonable, the cost of evaluating alternatives outweighs the benefit. The designer who sets the default has, in effect, already made the decision for the majority. This is why defaults carry ethical weight. A designer can claim to offer choice while structuring the choice so that most users never exercise it. Defaults are most powerful in one-time setup flows, where users move quickly and rarely return to revisit. Designers who want users to engage with settings should surface them at the moment of relevance, not bury them in preferences menus users open once and forget. Choosing the default is unavoidable. There is no neutral pre-selection. Every product that ships with a setting in place has already made a choice about whose interests that setting serves. Further reading The Power of Defaults — Jakob Nielsen, Nielsen Norman Group (2005) Defaults — The Decision Lab Status Quo Bias — The Decision Lab Choice Architecture 2.0: How People Interpret and Make Sense of Nudges — Job Krijnen, Behavioral Scientist (2018) Defaults Are Not the Same by Default — Jachimowicz, Duncan, Weber, and Johnson, Behavioral Scientist (2019) You just read why the pre-set option wins. So here’s one I’ve set for you: The reference designers keep open. Default Bias is 1 of 106 principles in Psychology of Design; the complete reference behind this newsletter. What attention does. How trust forms. Why habits stick. Each one written the way you just read this one: the mechanism, where it shows up, and how to use it. title: Double Booked
description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for October is WATER. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! Back in August, I tried a little experiment: publishing a question from my ongoing Icebreaker series as a stand-alone post, rather than a secondary item in the main newsletter. The hope was that this would encourage readers to actually answer in the comments. And it did! So I’m doing it again. All are welcome to chime in. Noticing is about other people, too. The Icebreaker series aims to help with that. There’s a central collection spot for all the icebreakers to date, here . Today’s icebreaker comes from me. What is the most recent, or most personally important, book that you’ve read twice (or more)? I would probably stipulate no children’s books; I think that’s a different discussion. But otherwise I’d be open to just seeing where the question leads — I think it’s somehow more interesting than just asking for someone’s “favorite” book. This subject of re-reading books has popped up randomly a couple of times for me lately, and made me think about how long it’s been since I’ve done it. I guess I now worry that I just don’t have enough time to repeat a book when there are so many I haven’t read once! That said, the most recent was The Ladies’ Paradise , by Zola, which I read for a second time about 10 years ago. The book I’ve read the most times is Native Son , three times (all in my 20s, I believe). What about you? Love to hear your thoughts! title: sua maior referência ☕️🐢
description: Quando me perguntam por referências pra desenvolver a criatividade, eu trapaceio 👀 Não falo sobre quem seguir. Conto como gosto de consumir: Em vez sempre de buscar nomes novos, experimenta se aprofundar nas suas Top 3 referências. Busca (ativamente) o nome delas no Youtube ou Spotify e ouvir entrevistas e conversas :¬) Ou seja, o contrário de juntos e shallow now (ehehe!): focar em se aprofundar em vez de conhecer de forma rasa. [ frase desse vídeo da Mica, do @comida.sem.regra ] Nossa geração tem essa chance - surreal! - de ter acesso à dicas e informações sobre as carreiras de quem nos inspira; mas 99% das pessoas consome só aquilo que os algoritmos mostram. Ditto isso: ontem esbarrei com o papo da Luiza com o Joan Miró . E, hoje, testei algo que ele contou sobre seu processo: criar em silêncio. Não porque é “melhor” (palavra que evito escrever sem aspas), ou por achar que isso me faria ter apenas ideias geniais. Foi curiosidade mesmo :¬) Gosto de testar estímulos e formas diferentes de criar e sentir como elas afetam o meu corpo, emoções, etc. [ a tradução acima contém ironia, hihi! ] E se você topar ser ~rebelde~, ignorar algoritmos e buscar uma conversas profundas de quem mais te inspira: O que te surpreendeu? Existem semelhanças entre vocês e os seus processos? Você discorda de algo que ela comentou ou acredita? Sentiu vontade de testar algo do processo criativo? garimpos 🐢 um carrossel meio aleatório , hihi! 👽 muito impressionado com esse mosaico. 👁️ essa designer cria piscinas maravilhosas. 💛 esse livro curtinho (±170 páginas) me prendeu muito da metade pra frente; a ponto de levá-lo pra academia e ler nos descansos. pum Esse é um pum curtinho. De tempos em tempos, é bom lembrar que não tomar alguma decisão (ou adiá-la) já é uma decisão :¬) Um conceito fácil de esquecer. E quando me lembro, algumas chavinhas são viradas por aqui. Com carinho, Tiago 🐢

Inspirar pessoas de contextos tão diferentes a expandirem suas zonas de conforto (aos pouquiiiiiiiiinhos) e viver uma vida criativa também estimula a minha criatividade. Meu 1º obrigado é por isso.
